concepts.name: Beating by a distance
concepts.description: "A beats B by d metres" means B is d metres short of the finish when A finishes.

concepts.name: Speed ratios from a race
concepts.description: In the same time, distances run are proportional to speeds.

concepts.name: Head starts and dead heats
concepts.description: A head start shortens the distance the slower runner has to cover.

concepts.name: Circular tracks
concepts.description: Runners on a loop meet when the faster has gained one full lap.

formulas.title: Beating by a distance
formulas.prompt: In a race of L metres, A beats B by d metres. How far has B run when A finishes?
formulas.formula:
A runs L, B runs L − d
(in the same time)
formulas.explanation: The race ends when A finishes; B is still d metres behind the line.
formulas.example: 100 m race, A beats B by 10 m → B has run 90 m
formulas.applicationPrompt: In a 200 m race A beats B by 40 m. How far has B run when A finishes?

formulas.title: Speed ratio
formulas.prompt: How do you get the ratio of speeds from "A beats B by d metres in L"?
formulas.formula: Speed of A : Speed of B = L : (L − d)
formulas.explanation: They run for equal time, so the distances are in the same ratio as the speeds.
formulas.example: 200 m race, A beats B by 40 m → 200 : 160 = 5 : 4
formulas.applicationPrompt: A beats B by 20 m in 100 m. What is the ratio of their speeds?

formulas.title: Head start
formulas.prompt: A gives B a start of s metres in a race of L metres and they finish together. What does each run?
formulas.formula:
A runs L, B runs L − s
Speed ratio = L : (L − s)
formulas.explanation: A dead heat means equal time, so it is the same as A beating B by s in an L-metre race.
formulas.example: 100 m race, 20 m start → A : B = 100 : 80 = 5 : 4
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the start to B's distance.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A gives B a 20 m start in a 100 m race and they tie. What is the ratio of their speeds?

formulas.title: Meeting on a circular track
formulas.prompt: Two runners start together on a circular track of length L. When do they next meet?
formulas.formula:
Same direction: t = L ÷ (S₁ − S₂)
Opposite direction: t = L ÷ (S₁ + S₂)
formulas.explanation: Same direction they meet when the faster gains one full lap; opposite directions they meet when together they cover one lap.
formulas.example: L = 400, speeds 5 and 3, same direction → 400 ÷ 2 = 200 s
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the speeds for same-direction running.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Runners at 5 and 3 m/s run the same way round a 400 m track. When do they next meet?

formulas.title: Combining two race results
formulas.prompt: In an L m race A beats B by x m and B beats C by y m. By how much does A beat C?
formulas.formula: A beats C by x + y − xy/L
formulas.explanation: When A finishes, C is behind B by y scaled down to B's distance, so less than x + y.
formulas.example: 100 m race, A beats B by 10 m and B beats C by 10 m: A beats C by 19 m (not 20).
formulas.applicationPrompt: In a km race A beats B by 100 m and B beats C by 100 m. By how much does A beat C?

formulas.title: Head start for a dead heat
formulas.prompt: A runs faster than B in the ratio a : b. What start should A give B so they finish together?
formulas.formula: Start = L × (1 − b/a) = L × (a − b) ÷ a
formulas.explanation: In the time A runs L, B runs L × b/a; the rest is the start B needs.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by b instead of a.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A runs 1.5 times as fast as B. On a 300 m course, what start should B get?

levels.title: Same Time, Different Distances
levels.description: What "beats by" and "head start" really mean.

blocks.title: The race stops when the winner finishes
blocks.body: "A beats B by 10 m in a 100 m race" means that at the instant A crosses the line, B is still 10 m short. So A ran 100 m and B ran 90 m — in exactly the same time.

blocks.title: Equal time, so distances give the ratio
blocks.body: Speed of A : Speed of B = L : (L − d)
blocks.caption: This one idea unlocks almost every race problem.

blocks.title: Head start = beating, seen from the other side
blocks.body: If A gives B a 20 m start in a 100 m race and they tie, then A runs 100 m while B runs 80 m. It is the same picture as A beating B by 20 m over 100 m.

levels.title: Races Formulas
levels.description: Beats-by, ratios, head starts and circular tracks.

levels.title: Times, Speeds and Starts
levels.description: Convert between time gaps, distances and speeds.

questions.question: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 10 m. How far has B run when A crosses the finishing line?
questions.explanation: B is 10 m short of the finish when A finishes, so B has run 100 − 10 = 90 m.
solutionSteps: B is 10 m behind the line.
questions.method: Distance run by the loser = L − d.

hints.text: Where is B when A finishes?

commonMistakes: Giving the beating distance (10) as the distance B ran.

questions.question: In a 200 m race, A beats B by 40 m. What is the ratio of the speed of A to the speed of B?
questions.explanation: When A has run 200 m, B has run 160 m in the same time. The ratio is 200 : 160 = 5 : 4.
solutionSteps: A runs 200 m, B runs 160 m in equal time.
questions.method: Ratio of speeds = ratio of distances in equal time.

hints.text: How far has B run when A finishes?
Same time, so speeds are in the ratio of distances.

commonMistakes: Giving the inverse ratio (4 : 5), or using 200 : 40.

questions.question: A runs 100 m in 20 seconds. When A finishes, B is 10 m behind. What is the speed of B, in m/s?
questions.explanation: B ran 90 m in the same 20 seconds, so his speed is 90 ÷ 20 = 4.5 m/s.
questions.method: Use the distance B actually ran and the time A took.

hints.text: B has run 90 m by the time A finishes.
Both have run for 20 seconds.

questions.question: A gives B a start of 20 m in a 100 m race and they finish together. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A runs 100 m and B runs 80 m in the same time
A runs 120 m and B runs 100 m in the same time
A and B run the same distance
A runs 80 m and B runs 100 m in the same time

questions.explanation: B starts 20 m ahead, so B only has to run 80 m while A runs the full 100 m — in equal time because they tie.
solutionSteps: A starts at 0, B starts at the 20 m mark.
A runs 100 m, B runs 80 m.
questions.method: The start reduces the runner's distance.

hints.text: A head start moves B closer to the finish.

commonMistakes: Adding the start to B's distance.

questions.question: The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 4. In a 500 m race, by how many metres does A beat B?
questions.explanation: When A runs 500 m, B runs 4/5 of that: 400 m. A wins by 500 − 400 = 100 m.

hints.text: In equal time, how far does B run when A runs 500 m?

commonMistakes: Giving 400 m, the distance B ran.

questions.question: In a 1000 m race, A finishes in 200 seconds and beats B by 50 seconds. By how many metres does A beat B?
questions.explanation: B takes 250 s for 1000 m, so B runs at 4 m/s. In the last 50 seconds B would cover 4 × 50 = 200 m. A wins by 200 m.
questions.method: A time gap converts to distance at the loser's speed.

hints.text: How long does B take for the full race?
What distance does B cover in the 50-second gap?

commonMistakes: Using A's speed (5 m/s) to convert the time gap.

questions.question: A runs at 8 m/s and B at 6 m/s. A gives B a start of 40 m and they reach the finish at the same moment. How long is the race?
solutionSteps: Time for A = L ÷ 8; time for B = (L − 40) ÷ 6.
questions.method: Equal times: L ÷ S_A = (L − s) ÷ S_B.

hints.text: A tie means equal times.
Write both times and set them equal.

commonMistakes: Adding the start to B's distance (giving 320 m, or a wrong balance).

questions.question: In a kilometre race A beats B by 100 m. If A's speed is 5 m/s, what is B's speed, in m/s?
questions.explanation: A runs 1000 m in 200 s. In that time B runs 900 m, so B's speed is 900 ÷ 200 = 4.5 m/s.

hints.text: How long does A take for the race?
How far has B run in that time?

questions.question: In a 100 m race A beats B by 20 m, and in a 100 m race B beats C by 10 m. By how many metres does A beat C in a 100 m race?
questions.explanation: When A runs 100 m, B runs 80 m. When B runs 100 m, C runs 90 m, so when B runs 80 m, C runs 80 × 90/100 = 72 m. A beats C by 100 − 72 = 28 m.
solutionSteps: B : C = 100 : 90, so in 80 m B-distance C runs 72 m.
questions.method: Chain the ratios; the two margins do not simply add.

hints.text: Use B as the bridge between A and C.
When A finishes, B is at 80 m — how far is C then?

questions.question: In a 1 km race A beats B by 100 m, and B beats C by 100 m over 1 km. By how many metres does A beat C over 1 km?
questions.explanation: When A has run 1000 m, B has run 900 m. When B runs 1000 m, C runs 900, so when B has run 900 m, C has run 810 m. A beats C by 1000 − 810 = 190 m.
solutionSteps: B : C = 1000 : 900, so C runs 900 × 0.9 = 810 m when B runs 900 m.
questions.method: Multiply the ratios rather than adding the margins.

hints.text: The second 100 m is a fraction of B's distance, not of 1000.
How far has C run when B has run 900 m?

commonMistakes: Adding the margins to get 200 m.

questions.question: Two runners start together from the same point of a 400 m circular track and run in the same direction at 5 m/s and 3 m/s. After how many seconds do they first meet again, anywhere on the track?
questions.explanation: The faster runner gains 2 m/s. To meet again the gain must be one full lap of 400 m: 400 ÷ 2 = 200 seconds.
questions.method: Same direction: lap length ÷ difference of speeds.

hints.text: Same direction: do you use the sum or the difference of the speeds?
The faster runner must gain exactly one lap.

commonMistakes: Working out when they are next together at the start (400 s), which is a different question.

questions.question: A can run 1 km in 3 min 10 s and B can run 1 km in 3 min 20 s. How many metres' start should A give B in a 1 km race so that they finish at the same moment (a dead heat)?
questions.explanation: A takes 3 min 10 s = 190 s for 1 km and B takes 3 min 20 s = 200 s. For a dead heat B may run only for A's 190 s. B's speed is 1000 ÷ 200 = 5 m/s, so in 190 s B covers 950 m. B must start 1000 − 950 = 50 m ahead.
solutionSteps: A: 190 s for 1000 m. B: 200 s for 1000 m.
In A's 190 s, B runs 5 × 190 = 950 m.
questions.method: Start = distance the slower runner cannot cover in the faster runner's time.

hints.text: Convert both times to seconds.
How far does B run in the 190 s that A needs?
The start makes up the rest of the 1000 m.

commonMistakes: Using A's speed for the 10-second gap (52.6 m) instead of B's.
Answering in seconds (10) instead of metres.

questions.question: A and B start together from the same point on a 300 m circular track and run in opposite directions at 5 m/s and 3 m/s. After how many seconds are they both at the starting point together for the first time?
questions.explanation: Being together at the starting point needs both runners to have finished a whole number of laps. A completes a lap every 300 ÷ 5 = 60 s and B every 300 ÷ 3 = 100 s. The first time both are back at the start is LCM(60, 100) = 300 s. Running in opposite directions does not change this, though it does make them pass each other much earlier, at 37.5 s.
solutionSteps: Both are at the start only at multiples of both lap times.
questions.method: Meeting at the starting point: LCM of the lap times, whatever the directions.

hints.text: When is each runner back at the starting point?
Find each runner's lap time.
They are at the start together at a common multiple of the lap times.

commonMistakes: Answering the first meeting anywhere on the track, 300 ÷ (5 + 3) = 37.5 s.
Multiplying the lap times (6000 s) instead of taking their LCM.
